{"id": "1:2/q16", "question": "Why is the Fātiḥa given its names?", "turns_on": "The titles are explained by different functions and contents of the sūra.", "positions": [{"id": "1:2/q16/p1", "position": "It is the Opening of the Book and prayer.", "reasons": "TABRISI, d. 548 (سيبويه): The lām normally has fatḥa because it cannot begin with sukun; lām of possession and emphasis are distinguished, and attached pronouns restore its original opening vowel. IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 (author): Rabb means owner; for a created being the title is used only in a construct phrase such as owner of the house or servant. IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 (أهل النظر): The derivation of ʿālam from ʿalāma, “sign,” supports the speculative theologians' view: the world is named as a sign pointing to its Creator. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (author): Saba’s statement that everything in the heavens and earth belongs to God is another subset within the universal lordship named in the Fātiḥa. | mentions 34:1 RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (author): Only God is necessary in Himself; everything else is possible and is called the world because its existence points to God. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (author): The opening glorification reveals the lights of divine majesty and moves from declaring God's transcendence to praising Him. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Rabb may derive from nurture: God manages and raises creation; stepdaughters are called rabāʾib because a husband raises them, making Rabb an attribute of action, while owner or master is an attribute of essence. | mentions 4:23 QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): With the definite article, Rabb belongs exclusively to God; without it, people may be called a household’s lord. God alone creates and provides, owns both owners and owned things, and cannot lose His dominion. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (الهروي): Rabb also means one who repairs, manages, restores, or takes care of something; rabbani scholars are named for tending to scripture. NASAFI, d. 710 (author): Al-‘alamin may mean everything the Creator knows of bodies, substances, and accidents, or every existing thing besides God, named for being evidence of His existence. ABUHAYYAN, d. 745 (author): Rabb may be a verbal noun used adjectivally or an active participle with deleted alif; as a title it is exclusive to God, while others require a possessive complement. SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 (author): The lām in li-llah expresses entitlement here; other senses include ownership, transfer, kinship, cause, address, oath exclamation, clarification, result, location, endpoint, elevation, and augmentation. | mentions 16:72, 4:105, 12:23, 28:8, 21:47, 17:78, 35:13, 17:109, 12:43, 11:107, 43:29, 16:1, 27:72, 8:9 IBNKATHIR, d. 774 (author): The unqualified title al-Rabb is used only for God; for other possessors it must be annexed, and some say al-Rabb is the greatest name. BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 (author): Al-Baqara is also called the Radiant and the Hump: it illuminates guidance and sufficiency, brightens believers' faces at judgment, and exalts belief in the afterlife above every other good after monotheism. ITQAN, d. 911 (author): By signaling all Qur’anic aims, the Fatiha achieves an exemplary opening and combines beautiful words, pleasing cadence, and rhetorical forms. BURSEVI, d. 1127 (author): It is called the Treasure surah because a report says the Opening is a treasure from God's Throne. ALUSI, d. 1270 (author): The opening of al-Fātiḥa is also the final wording of the supplications in 10:10, giving the sūra a return-to-the-beginning frame. | mentions 10:10 ALUSI, d. 1270 (author): Opening the sūra’s descriptions with Rabb al-ʿālamīn suits the Prophet’s mission and asks for compassion toward all creatures, since God is their Lord. ALUSI, d. 1270 (ابن حلزة): Ibn Ḥilaza’s poem calls al-Mundhir rabb, an unusual unqualified application of the title to a human being.
